newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks seen up if poll offers strong govt.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks seen up if poll offers strong govt.

text.p: The Thai stock market is set to gain if Sunday's general election offers the possibility of a strong government, irrespective of which of the two key political parties wins, analysts sad on Friday.
However, they noted that the temptation to take profits might be strong next week after heavy gains made this week.

"First of all the market's fundamentally cheap and providing the election gives a result with a government or possible government which offers stability and which satisfies the forex markets...I think it will be up," said Richard Henderson, head of Research at Krungthai Thanakit.

The election is seen as close contest between the Democrat Party headed by former Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai and Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's New Aspiration Party (NAP). If either of them wins, they will have not have enough seats to form a coalition government and must link up with other parties.
Historically, no single party has won previous elections outright and a coalition government has always ruled.
The SET Index rose 10.11 points on Friday to cross the key 1,000-point level at 1000.73.
During a volatile week of trading the index gained 88.01 points.
The Democrats are seen as popular with the business community because they have a strong economic team offering to pull Thailand out of a sluggish economic year.
But some brokers said the market would welcome whichever party won so long as it offered a strong administration.

"Whoever wins will be positive to the market and I think we will test 1100 by the end of the year, though investors will have to be careful about profit taking next week," said a senior trader at Asia Credit.
"Foreigners will drive the market next week with the retailers following whichever way they go."
Rob Collins, head of research at Asia Equity, said the short term implications of the Democrat Party emerging as the largest party could help put 30 points on the market index.
He said the reverse was true if the NAP looked most likely to form the next government.
"When the market is up everybody says it doesn't matter and tells you to come piling in but I think it does matter."
He said the implications of a close result were not positive given the weaker nature of a resulting coalition, which would be more reliant on fickle political allies.
Collins said there were negative longer term consequences of an NAP victory. The NAP contains many defectors from other parties and analysts are worried about its cohesiveness should it rule.
